corrected_claim.text: Wiedrich's battery stood on a hill north of the Baltimore turnpike near the cemetery and east of the town (Hunt: in front of the cemetery entrance). During the afternoon it skirmished with a rebel battery posted near the York road. About 5 p.m., when the Union infantry that had advanced through the town was repulsed, Wiedrich changed the direction of his pieces, opened with shells on the columns advancing from the town, and then fired canister at the enemy that appeared in front; the fire was kept up until late in the evening. Howard and Hunt place the enemy's single attempt to turn the right at about 4.30 p.m. and say Wiedrich's battery broke the line. Nothing in the reports ties this fire to the railroad cut (the cut lies on Oak Ridge, far from his front).

corrected_claim.text: At 5.25 p.m. Hancock wrote from the cemetery: when he arrived 'an hour since' he found the troops had given up the front of Gettysburg and the town; the troops had taken a position in the cemetery that 'cannot well be taken' but is easily turned; Slocum was coming on the ground and taking position on the right; there were no troops on the left, the Third Corps not having reported; Gibbon had better march up to a commanding position on the right or left; the battle was quiet and he thought all would be right until night; trains had been sent back; 'I think we can retire; if not, we can fight here, as the ground appears not unfavorable with good troops'; he would soon transfer the command to Slocum. corrected_claim.text: Slocum moved the corps to Two Taverns on the morning of Jul 1 and resumed the march when news came that the First and Eleventh Corps were engaged. Geary, at Two Taverns by 11 a.m., advanced at about 3 p.m., reported to Hancock, who sent him to the extreme left, and by 5 p.m. had two regiments of his First Brigade on the hills south and west of the town, the rest along the line to the Baltimore turnpike and the Second Brigade with two guns in reserve about 2 miles out; the division rested on its arms during the night. Williams' division was directed by a cross-road toward the Hanover road to take an eminence about a mile east of the town, found it held by the enemy and, when about to assault, was called back as the Union forces had retired behind the town; it bivouacked nearer the Baltimore pike. The seed's 'Geary takes position on Cemetery Ridge' and '17:30' do not match the reports (the left near Round Top; 15:00 advance, 17:00 in position).

corrected_claim.text: The seed's order of events is corrected: at Two Taverns Williams learned that the First and Eleventh Corps were engaged (not yet that they had retired); the division then moved up the pike and turned by a cross-road toward the Hanover road to seize a commanding hill east of the town; the hill was found held by the enemy and, when the division was about to assault, it was ordered to withdraw because the Union forces had retired behind the town. It then took a position nearer the Baltimore pike and bivouacked; Ruger puts the move to a position three-quarters of a mile to the rear 'about sunset'. Slocum turned the temporary command of the corps over to Williams and Ruger took the division. The reports do not name Culp's Hill for the hill east of the town.

corrected_claim.text: Grover (7th Indiana) reports that on the afternoon of Jul 1, by Wadsworth's order, the regiment took position on the hill east of Gettysburg, then the extreme right of the Union line, and began a temporary breastwork; during the following night a force of the enemy attempted to penetrate the line but was easily driven off, supposing itself confronted by a heavy force; on the night of the 1st Sergeant Hussey, unassisted, captured a lieutenant of the 25th Virginia and drove off a squad of 20 men. Ewell reports that Johnson, after forming his line on this side of the wooded hill, sent a reconnoitering party to it; near the summit it was met by a superior force that captured part of it while the rest escaped; Johnson therefore refrained from taking the hill and, at daybreak, it was too late for a change. The tie between the two accounts is an inference; the seed's 'and man' (a second prisoner) is not in Grover's report.

corrected_claim.text: Hancock says Wadsworth's division and a battery were placed on the eminence just across the turnpike, which the division held to the end of the operations, and that he sent Geary's division to the high ground near Round Top. Doubleday records that Hancock directed him to send a force to support a battery on a lower range of hills about 100 yards east of the cemetery position and that he sent the rest of Wadsworth's division there, after which orders from Howard, who ranked Hancock, to send the troops in another direction caused some delay and confusion. Howard says Hancock was to arrange the troops and place the batteries on the left of the Baltimore pike while he took the right, and that Wadsworth's division was sent to a height to the right and rear. Wadsworth: on the evening of the 1st he was ordered to occupy a hill on the right of the cemetery. Hancock's exact words to Wadsworth are not in any report. The seed's 'Little Round Top' is Hancock's 'Round Top Mountain' (Geary, T1-176).

Howard: Hancock to arrange the troops and place the batteries on the left of the Baltimore pike, Howard the right; Wadsworth's division was sent to a height to the right and rear
Wadsworth: on the evening of the 1st the division was ordered to occupy a hill on the right of the cemetery
Halstead (Doubleday's staff): Hancock, who arrived under orders from Meade to assume the command, 'ordered Wadsworth at once to Culp's Hill to secure that important position'

corrected_claim.text: Johnson, marching from Scotland by the Cashtown road, did not arrive in time to take part in the fighting. Nicholls' brigade, in front, was at about 7 o'clock on the Cashtown road marching toward Gettysburg when Johnson ordered it east along the railroad about three-quarters of a mile from the town. Jones's brigade left camp at 7 a.m., reached the town 'late in the afternoon', passed the depot to the left of the town and formed line about dark; Richardson (42nd Virginia) puts the arrival 'about sunset'; Steuart's brigade came 'toward evening' and, marching through part of the town and along the York railroad, formed line to the northeast; Walker's brigade arrived on the evening and took position after nightfall on the southeast side of the town near the Hanover road, on Culp's farm. Johnson himself: 'late on the night of July 1' he formed line of battle in a ravine in an open field, Nicholls on the right next Jones, Steuart and Walker on the left, pickets well to the front, the troops sleeping on their arms. Lee: Johnson 'did not reach Gettysburg until a late hour'. All of these are carried as the arrival window; no single hour is picked.

corrected_claim.text: Lee wrote that Ewell was instructed to carry the hill occupied by the enemy if he found it practicable, but to avoid a general engagement until the other divisions arrived; Ewell decided to await Johnson's division, which reached Gettysburg at a late hour, and the enemy meanwhile occupied the point Ewell meant to seize. Ewell wrote that on entering the town he received a message from the commanding general to attack the hill if he could do so to advantage; he could not bring artillery to bear, all the troops with him were jaded by twelve hours' marching and fighting, Cemetery Hill was not assailable from the town, and he determined to take a wooded hill to his left with Johnson's division. Early's report: he rode to urge an immediate advance, sent word to Hill that if he would send a division the hill could be taken, learned that Johnson was coming and that it was determined to occupy a wooded hill to the left of Cemetery Hill, but the division arrived late and 'no effort ... was made that night'. In 1877 Early added the reasons he knew: Rodes' division had lost about 2,500, only two of his own brigades were available, and constant reports of an enemy advance on the York road. The seed's 'narrow streets' and 'lack of support from Hill' do not appear in the reports; Early's 1877 paper has Hill's troops not advanced beyond Seminary Ridge. The seed's 'Early opposes' is corrected in T1-187.

corrected_claim.text: Early's report: before he found Ewell, Rodes or Hill he rode into the town to urge an immediate advance; Smith's aide brought word that a large force was advancing on the York road and, though Early had no faith in the report, he sent Gordon with his brigade to take charge of Smith's also and watch the road; he sent word to Hill that a division could take the hill; told that Johnson was coming, it was determined to take the wooded hill to the left of Cemetery Hill; Johnson arrived at a late hour and no effort was made that night. corrected_claim.text: The National Park Service landscape report says: troops began to arrive on Cemetery Hill on July 1 when Howard posted a reserve of his Eleventh Corps (Steinwehr's division); late in the day, as Union troops retreated, they reinforced the defensive lines around Cemetery Hill; lines of artillery were positioned near the summit along the northern and western borders of Evergreen Cemetery with caissons and horses among the grave plots; it was reported that General Howard ordered troops to lay the headstones flat on the ground to prevent their destruction; troops tore down wood and stone fences and rebuilt stone fences as breastworks. Battle damage included bullet holes and cracks in some grave markers, damage to grave-plot fences, removal of planks from the fences along the Baltimore pike, and a damaged gatehouse. The report does not date the laying flat of the headstones or the fence damage within the three days, says nothing of 'iron fences', and names no monument destroyed. The seed's attribution of the night of Jul 1 is therefore not documented; the damage is shown as occurring during the battle, with the evening of Jul 1 as the earliest time.

corrected_claim.text: On Jul 1 Greene's brigade was posted on the left with the division, about half a mile to the right of Sugar Loaf Mountain in front of the Taneytown road, with 'no incidents to note'; the division rested on its arms during the night. On Jul 2 Geary was relieved by the Third Corps and at 5 a.m. placed his division on the right of the centre of the line; Greene took position at about 6 a.m. on the crest of the hill and 'as soon as we were in position, we began to intrench ourselves and throw up breastworks'. Godard (60th New York): at or about 6 a.m. the regiment assumed position and threw up intrenchments by Greene's order, working until about 9 a.m. when they were completed; Ireland (137th): the breastworks were completed about noon; Hammerstein (78th): a breastwork of trees and dirt was soon thrown up; Stegman (102nd): the men were ordered to build breastworks of cord-wood and rock. Greene's report prints 'By 13 o'clock we had a good cover for the men'; '13' is not an hour and the reading '10' is a conjecture not checked against the scan. The seed's 'construction began the night of Jul 1-2' (New York state agency page) is contradicted by Greene's and Geary's own accounts; the 'done about noon' (Gettysburg Daily) agrees with Ireland for one regiment.

corrected_claim.text: Butterfield's order of 1.10 p.m.: Hancock to turn over the Second Corps to Gibbon, go to the front and, if Reynolds is dead, 'assume command of the corps there assembled, viz, the Eleventh, First, and Third, at Emmitsburg', advising Meade whether the ground is a better one to fight on. Hancock: at 3 p.m. he arrived at Gettysburg and assumed command; Wadsworth's division and a battery were placed on the eminence across the turnpike. Howard (dispatch): Hancock arrived at 4 p.m. Halstead (Doubleday's staff): Wadsworth led the 7th Indiana to Culp's Hill; Hancock, received at the hill, ordered Wadsworth at once to Culp's Hill to secure the position. Doubleday: Hancock directed him to send a force to support a battery on a lower range of hills some 100 yards east; he sent the rest of Wadsworth's division, then Howard's counter-orders caused delay. Smith: his brigade, formed in mass in rear of the hill, advanced through the cemetery to the front of the hill overlooking the town; its arrival 'in good order and with full ranks' contributed to holding the hill. The seed's 'about 1,600 fresh' and 'tells Doubleday to send every man' are not in these reports; the arrival hours 15:00, before 16:00, 16:00 and 16:30 are carried as scenarios under the recorded default C-039 (about 15:00-16:00).

corrected_claim.text: The corps' approach is as in T1-176: Geary advanced about 3 p.m., was sent by Hancock to the high ground near Round Top and by 5 p.m. was on the extreme left (so the seed's 'Cemetery Ridge' and its conflict with Geary at Culp's Hill on Jul 2 at 05:00 are resolved: Geary moved from the left to the right at 5 a.m. on Jul 2); Williams' division was called back and bivouacked near the Baltimore pike. The command: Hancock says he transferred it to Slocum between 5 and 6 o'clock; Howard writes that Hancock's written order reached him at 7 when Slocum had just arrived, and Meade and Howard have Slocum and Sickles at the cemetery about 7 p.m.; both are carried (T1-177). The seed's 'Hancock tells Slocum that Meade ordered him to take command' is not in Hancock's report or dispatch (he wrote that he would 'communicate with Slocum and transfer the command'); it is carried as unsupported in that wording.
